paras: The killing of Gaither Reese was the fatal shooting of Reese, of Spring Creek in Madison County, North Carolina, in March 1888 by a party of Haywood County men led by Jerome Ruff, who were trying to arrest him on a Haywood capias. Four men were indicted for murder, the case was moved to Buncombe County and continued, and Ruff remained at large under a $200 reward offered by the governor. The Asheville Citizen called it "a horrible murder" and argued that an officer had no right to shoot a man accused only of a misdemeanor who tried to escape.

According to a Spring Creek correspondent of the Asheville Citizen, a capias had been issued in Haywood County for Reese's arrest, and he had fled into Madison County. The process was placed in the hands of Jerome Ruff and Pink Kirkpatrick of Haywood, who, "thinking they had a right to make the arrest in Madison county," summoned Charles Rice and C. Coward and told them they would be fined if they did not go. The Citizen later described Ruff as an officer of Haywood County and said Reese had been charged, "we believe," with a misdemeanor. Its first report, drawn from visitors from Madison County, added that "a slight difficulty" had occurred between Reese and Ruff some time earlier.

The Citizen dated the shooting to Friday, the 23rd of March. The party went to the place of Joe Plemons, where Reese was, and on recognizing them he started to run. The correspondent wrote that two guns were fired and a ball struck Reese in the back of the head, killing him instantly, while the first report said the men carried rifles and lodged several balls in him.

Ruff fled at once to Haywood County, while Kirkpatrick, Coward and Rice were arrested and given a hearing before Esquire Jasper Ebbs. Ebbs committed Rice and Kirkpatrick to the Madison jail and held Coward in $500 for his appearance at court.

Excitement continued in parts of Madison County, and in April a state paper reported that men were scouring the country where Ruff was thought to be hiding. At the Madison Superior Court in Marshall in the summer of 1888, the grand jury returned true bills for murder against Jerome Ruff, Charles Price, Pinkney Kirkpatrick and Columbus Coward, all described as young men of Haywood County.

Defense counsel, among them J. C. L. Gudger and Garland S. Ferguson of Waynesville, filed affidavits that the men could not safely be tried in Madison. The State answered only that Reese's widowed mother, from what the Citizen called one of the most powerful families in Madison, had exhausted her resources employing counsel for the prosecution, and Judge Boykin removed the case to Buncombe County. When the case was called in Buncombe Superior Court in mid-August, Solicitor Moody won a continuance because State witnesses were in Tennessee, and the defendants were allowed bail of $2,000 each. In October the governor offered $200 for Ruff, and no report of a trial or verdict appears in the coverage.

Coverage centered on the Asheville Citizen, which headlined its first report "A Horrible Murder in Madison" and its second "The Madison Murder," with the deck "An Outrageous Affair." Its editorial note called the killing "a very gross outrage" for which the guilty should be severely punished, adding that "The law allows nothing of the kind." By August the paper's tone was more measured: it praised the defense arguments and noted that three of the accused had stayed nearby, apparently believing the killing was done under warrant of law.

Outside the state, a one-line wire item said only that Reese "was shot and killed while trying to escape from a Deputy Sheriff and his posse," with no charge or name for the shooters. The item ran in early April in Arkansas, Missouri, Mississippi and Kansas papers, usually dated "on the 30th." No paper stated Reese's race; the only racial label in the coverage is the governor's notice describing Ruff as white.

The date varies: the Citizen's local reports, written within a week, placed the killing on Friday the 23rd, the wire copies said "the 30th," possibly the dispatch date, and the governor's reward notice said "the 2d of March." Ruff's standing also shifted: the first report called him only the leader of "the gang," while later items called him "Deputy Sheriff Ruff" or an officer holding process.

reader.title: Killing of Gaither Reese
bases: Reese was shot while fleeing a party of four Haywood men led by Jerome Ruff, called an officer or deputy sheriff, who held a capias for his arrest and had summoned two of the others (A2, A3, A11).

Two separate local accounts in the Asheville Citizen (visitors from Madison and a Spring Creek correspondent) agree on the shooting, and the wire item, court reports and governor's reward confirm it (A1, A2, A5, A11, A13).

framing.detail: Asheville Citizen headlines 'A Horrible Murder in Madison' and 'The Madison Murder. An Outrageous Affair'; editorial says the law does not allow shooting a fleeing misdemeanant.
One-line wire brief in out-of-state news columns presents the killing as an escape from a deputy sheriff and posse.
Asheville Citizen's August court report praises defense counsel and notes the defendants believed they acted under warrant of law.
Charlotte Democrat lists the reward for Ruff among the governor's rewards for murderers.

conflicts.note: The Citizen's reports, written within a week from local sources, are closest to the event; the wire's 'the 30th' may be the date of the dispatch, and the reward notice came seven months later.
